case_info.scenario: A 17-year-old male with an unremarkable medical history presented with 2 days of painless blurred vision in the right eye. Three weeks prior, he was admitted with fever, myalgias, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and truncal rash. Laboratory evaluation revealed leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Heterophile antibody test results were negative. He recovered with supportive treatment. On examination, the patient was well appearing. His best-corrected visual acuity in the affected right eye was 20/25 and baseline count fingers in the left, secondary to amblyopia. His intraocular pressures were normal and extraocular movements were full. Examination was notable for 1+ anterior chamber cell in the right eye. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye revealed vitreous cell and a supratemporal branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) abutting the fovea. Multiple retinal nerve fiber layer infarcts were observed bilaterally throughout the posterior pole and retinal periphery. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated multifocal areas of retinal arteriolar and capillary nonperfusion, more so in the right eye than the left. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the right eye showed loss of inner retinal laminations, presumably due to intracellular swelling of the ganglion cell layer within areas of retinal arteriolar and capillary nonperfusion (Figure 1). Late vascular staining appeared limited to venules at the boundary of perfused and nonperfused retina and scattered areas of capillary nonperfusion. The patient denied intravenous drug use or antecedent trauma.

case_info.answer: Order serologic infectious and inflammatory workup
case_info.caption: A, Optical coherence tomography (OCT) through the white retinal lesions (pink line) shows focal inner retinal thickening (pink arrowheads). The blue line denotes the OCT through the macula, highlighting loss of inner retinal organization temporal to the macula due to ischemia from the retinal circulation. B, The corresponding fluorescein angiography with white arrowheads highlights the peripheral retina nonperfusion associated with the branch retinal artery occlusion. The insert shows a late-stage frame at 12 minutes with vascular staining and leakage.
case_info.explanation: C. Order serologic infectious and inflammatory workup While most retinal artery occlusions are embolic, the current presentation is atypical. The patient experienced vision loss in his remaining good eye and inpatient workup may be prudent. Local steroid injection is not advisable before thorough systemic evaluation. Option D is lower yield considering the presentation. The patient was admitted for systemic evaluation. Branch retinal artery occlusions have a variety of etiologies, including embolic, vasospastic, vasculitic, and coagulopathic.1Older patients with embolic risk factors are the typical demographic. BRAOs are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population.2Carotid doppler, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging brain results were normal. Complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. International normalized ratio was 1.2, mildly elevated. Partial thromboplastin time was normal. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) was considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions in a young patient without known risk factors. Testing revealed positive lupus anticoagulant and high titer β-2 glycoprotein immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) (>150 standard IgG and IgM units). Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activity were normal and factor V Leiden mutation was negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a low titer, 1:40. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. This patient presented 3 weeks after a febrile illness of uncertain etiology. A postinfectious process was suspected due to the timing of symptom onset and prompt resolution of systemic symptoms. An infectious workup was nonetheless initiated. Syphilis, tuberculosis, and toxoplasma serology results were negative.Bartonellawas considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions, history of lymphadenopathy, and substantial prior cat exposure.BartonellaIgG test results were positive (1:32 768 titer) and IgM results were negative. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgG results were positive (>750 U/mL viral capsid antigen antibody, 510 U/mL nuclear antibody) and IgM were negative. Cytomegalovirus IgG and HIV results were negative. West Nile Virus IgG and IgM were negative. APS is characterized by autoantibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and β-glycoprotein) with systemic thrombotic sequelae.3It can develop following systemic infections including HIV, cytomegalovirus, EBV, hepatitis, andBartonella.4The incidence of APS is approximately 5 in 100 000 persons per year.5The pathophysiology for development of APS is unclear. Furthermore, antibodies can be transient or persistent. The patient’s antibodies were retested after 3 months and revealed persistently high titers confirming the diagnosis. APS management revolves around prevention of thrombotic events by anticoagulation.6In rare cases, catastrophic APS may cause multiple organ failure and be a fatal disease.7Though the infectious trigger remains unclear (EBV andBartonellaare possibilities), we suspect APS to be a driving factor in the patient’s presentation. The patient received therapeutically dosed enoxaparin and aspirin. Additionally, he received solumedrol intravenously with transition to oral prednisone. Retinal perfusion improved. Infectious disease was consulted and recommended a 4-week course of doxycycline and rifampin due to suspicion that the patient’s preceding febrile illness was secondary toBartonella. In follow-up, the patient’s right eye visual acuity remained stable at 20/25 with no new occlusions and gradual resolution of retinal lesions (Figure 2).

Given the patient's prior symptoms suggestive of a viral illness, the recent presentation of retinal findings, and the observation of retinal vascular occlusion, it is crucial to investigate possible underlying infectious causes such as viral retinitis or other vascular inflammatory conditions. This approach could inform further treatment decisions and manage any potentially treatable causes of the vascular changes observed.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

A 17-year-old male with an unremarkable medical history presented with 2 days of painless blurred vision in the right eye. Three weeks prior, he was admitted with fever, myalgias, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and truncal rash. Laboratory evaluation revealed leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Heterophile antibody test results were negative. He recovered with supportive treatment. On examination, the patient was well appearing. His best-corrected visual acuity in the affected right eye was 20/25 and baseline count fingers in the left, secondary to amblyopia. His intraocular pressures were normal and extraocular movements were full. Examination was notable for 1+ anterior chamber cell in the right eye. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye revealed vitreous cell and a supratemporal branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) abutting the fovea. Multiple retinal nerve fiber layer infarcts were observed bilaterally throughout the posterior pole and retinal periphery. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated multifocal areas of retinal arteriolar and capillary nonperfusion, more so in the right eye than the left. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the right eye showed loss of inner retinal laminations, presumably due to intracellular swelling of the ganglion cell layer within areas of retinal arteriolar and capillary nonperfusion (Figure 1). Late vascular staining appeared limited to venules at the boundary of perfused and nonperfused retina and scattered areas of capillary nonperfusion. The patient denied intravenous drug use or antecedent trauma.

Branch retinal artery occlusions have a variety of etiologies, including embolic, vasospastic, vasculitic, and coagulopathic.1Older patients with embolic risk factors are the typical demographic. BRAOs are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population.2Carotid doppler, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging brain results were normal. Complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. International normalized ratio was 1.2, mildly elevated. Partial thromboplastin time was normal. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) was considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions in a young patient without known risk factors. Testing revealed positive lupus anticoagulant and high titer β-2 glycoprotein immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) (>150 standard IgG and IgM units). Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activity were normal and factor V Leiden mutation was negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a low titer, 1:40. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. This patient presented 3 weeks after a febrile illness of uncertain etiology. A postinfectious process was suspected due to the timing of symptom onset and prompt resolution of systemic symptoms. An infectious workup was nonetheless initiated. Syphilis, tuberculosis, and toxoplasma serology results were negative.Bartonellawas considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions, history of lymphadenopathy, and substantial prior cat exposure.BartonellaIgG test results were positive (1:32 768 titer) and IgM results were negative. West Nile Virus IgG and IgM were negative. Furthermore, antibodies can be transient or persistent. The patient’s antibodies were retested after 3 months and revealed persistently high titers confirming the diagnosis. APS management revolves around prevention of thrombotic events by anticoagulation.6In rare cases, catastrophic APS may cause multiple organ failure and be a fatal disease.7Though the infectious trigger remains unclear (EBV andBartonellaare possibilities), we suspect APS to be a driving factor in the patient’s presentation. You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]

[Interaction Guidelines]

2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]

Three weeks prior, he was admitted with fever, myalgias, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and truncal rash. Laboratory evaluation revealed leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Heterophile antibody test results were negative. He recovered with supportive treatment. On examination, the patient was well appearing. His best-corrected visual acuity in the affected right eye was 20/25 and baseline count fingers in the left, secondary to amblyopia. His intraocular pressures were normal and extraocular movements were full. Examination was notable for 1+ anterior chamber cell in the right eye. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye revealed vitreous cell and a supratemporal branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) abutting the fovea. Multiple retinal nerve fiber layer infarcts were observed bilaterally throughout the posterior pole and retinal periphery. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated multifocal areas of retinal arteriolar and capillary nonperfusion, more so in the right eye than the left. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the right eye showed loss of inner retinal laminations, presumably due to intracellular swelling of the ganglion cell layer within areas of retinal arteriolar and capillary nonperfusion (Figure 1). Late vascular staining appeared limited to venules at the boundary of perfused and nonperfused retina and scattered areas of capillary nonperfusion. [Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:

  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the

  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 2.5. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: C. Order serologic infectious and inflammatory workup While most retinal artery occlusions are embolic, the current presentation is atypical. The patient experienced vision loss in his remaining good eye and inpatient workup may be prudent. Local steroid injection is not advisable before thorough systemic evaluation. Option D is lower yield considering the presentation. The patient was admitted for systemic evaluation. Branch retinal artery occlusions have a variety of etiologies, including embolic, vasospastic, vasculitic, and coagulopathic.1Older patients with embolic risk factors are the typical demographic. BRAOs are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population.2Carotid doppler, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging brain results were normal. Complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. International normalized ratio was 1.2, mildly elevated. Partial thromboplastin time was normal. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) was considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions in a young patient without known risk factors. Testing revealed positive lupus anticoagulant and high titer β-2 glycoprotein immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) (>150 standard IgG and IgM units). Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activity were normal and factor V Leiden mutation was negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a low titer, 1:40. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. This patient presented 3 weeks after a febrile illness of uncertain etiology. A postinfectious process was suspected due to the timing of symptom onset and prompt resolution of systemic symptoms. An infectious workup was nonetheless initiated. Syphilis, tuberculosis, and toxoplasma serology results were negative.Bartonellawas considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions, history of lymphadenopathy, and substantial prior cat exposure.BartonellaIgG test results were positive (1:32 768 titer) and IgM results were negative. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgG results were positive (>750 U/mL viral capsid antigen antibody, 510 U/mL nuclear antibody) and IgM were negative. Cytomegalovirus IgG and HIV results were negative. West Nile Virus IgG and IgM were negative. APS is characterized by autoantibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and β-glycoprotein) with systemic thrombotic sequelae.3It can develop following systemic infections including HIV, cytomegalovirus, EBV, hepatitis, andBartonella.4The incidence of APS is approximately 5 in 100 000 persons per year.5The pathophysiology for development of APS is unclear. Furthermore, antibodies can be transient or persistent. The patient’s antibodies were retested after 3 months and revealed persistently high titers confirming the diagnosis. APS management revolves around prevention of thrombotic events by anticoagulation.6In rare cases, catastrophic APS may cause multiple organ failure and be a fatal disease.7Though the infectious trigger remains unclear (EBV andBartonellaare possibilities), we suspect APS to be a driving factor in the patient’s presentation. The patient received therapeutically dosed enoxaparin and aspirin. Additionally, he received solumedrol intravenously with transition to oral prednisone. Retinal perfusion improved. Infectious disease was consulted and recommended a 4-week course of doxycycline and rifampin due to suspicion that the patient’s preceding febrile illness was secondary toBartonella. In follow-up, the patient’s right eye visual acuity remained stable at 20/25 with no new occlusions and gradual resolution of retinal lesions (Figure 2).

   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't

case_info.explanation: C. Order serologic infectious and inflammatory workup While most retinal artery occlusions are embolic, the current presentation is atypical. The patient experienced vision loss in his remaining good eye and inpatient workup may be prudent. Local steroid injection is not advisable before thorough systemic evaluation. Option D is lower yield considering the presentation. The patient was admitted for systemic evaluation. Branch retinal artery occlusions have a variety of etiologies, including embolic, vasospastic, vasculitic, and coagulopathic.1Older patients with embolic risk factors are the typical demographic. BRAOs are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population.2Carotid doppler, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging brain results were normal. Complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. International normalized ratio was 1.2, mildly elevated. Partial thromboplastin time was normal. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) was considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions in a young patient without known risk factors. Testing revealed positive lupus anticoagulant and high titer β-2 glycoprotein immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) (>150 standard IgG and IgM units). Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activity were normal and factor V Leiden mutation was negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a low titer, 1:40. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. This patient presented 3 weeks after a febrile illness of uncertain etiology. A postinfectious process was suspected due to the timing of symptom onset and prompt resolution of systemic symptoms. An infectious workup was nonetheless initiated. Syphilis, tuberculosis, and toxoplasma serology results were negative.Bartonellawas considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions, history of lymphadenopathy, and substantial prior cat exposure.BartonellaIgG test results were positive (1:32 768 titer) and IgM results were negative. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgG results were positive (>750 U/mL viral capsid antigen antibody, 510 U/mL nuclear antibody) and IgM were negative. Cytomegalovirus IgG and HIV results were negative. West Nile Virus IgG and IgM were negative. APS is characterized by autoantibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and β-glycoprotein) with systemic thrombotic sequelae.3It can develop following systemic infections including HIV, cytomegalovirus, EBV, hepatitis, andBartonella.4The incidence of APS is approximately 5 in 100 000 persons per year.5The pathophysiology for development of APS is unclear. Furthermore, antibodies can be transient or persistent. The patient’s antibodies were retested after 3 months and revealed persistently high titers confirming the diagnosis. APS management revolves around prevention of thrombotic events by anticoagulation.6In rare cases, catastrophic APS may cause multiple organ failure and be a fatal disease.7Though the infectious trigger remains unclear (EBV andBartonellaare possibilities), we suspect APS to be a driving factor in the patient’s presentation. The patient received therapeutically dosed enoxaparin and aspirin. Additionally, he received solumedrol intravenously with transition to oral prednisone. Retinal perfusion improved. Infectious disease was consulted and recommended a 4-week course of doxycycline and rifampin due to suspicion that the patient’s preceding febrile illness was secondary toBartonella. In follow-up, the patient’s right eye visual acuity remained stable at 20/25 with no new occlusions and gradual resolution of retinal lesions (Figure 2).

The patient denied intravenous drug use or antecedent trauma.

case_info.explanation: C. Order serologic infectious and inflammatory workup While most retinal artery occlusions are embolic, the current presentation is atypical. The patient experienced vision loss in his remaining good eye and inpatient workup may be prudent. Local steroid injection is not advisable before thorough systemic evaluation. Option D is lower yield considering the presentation. The patient was admitted for systemic evaluation. Branch retinal artery occlusions have a variety of etiologies, including embolic, vasospastic, vasculitic, and coagulopathic.1Older patients with embolic risk factors are the typical demographic. BRAOs are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population.2Carotid doppler, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging brain results were normal. Complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. International normalized ratio was 1.2, mildly elevated. Partial thromboplastin time was normal. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) was considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions in a young patient without known risk factors. Testing revealed positive lupus anticoagulant and high titer β-2 glycoprotein immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) (>150 standard IgG and IgM units). Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activity were normal and factor V Leiden mutation was negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a low titer, 1:40. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. This patient presented 3 weeks after a febrile illness of uncertain etiology. A postinfectious process was suspected due to the timing of symptom onset and prompt resolution of systemic symptoms. An infectious workup was nonetheless initiated. Syphilis, tuberculosis, and toxoplasma serology results were negative.Bartonellawas considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions, history of lymphadenopathy, and substantial prior cat exposure.BartonellaIgG test results were positive (1:32 768 titer) and IgM results were negative. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgG results were positive (>750 U/mL viral capsid antigen antibody, 510 U/mL nuclear antibody) and IgM were negative. Cytomegalovirus IgG and HIV results were negative. West Nile Virus IgG and IgM were negative. APS is characterized by autoantibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and β-glycoprotein) with systemic thrombotic sequelae.3It can develop following systemic infections including HIV, cytomegalovirus, EBV, hepatitis, andBartonella.4The incidence of APS is approximately 5 in 100 000 persons per year.5The pathophysiology for development of APS is unclear. Furthermore, antibodies can be transient or persistent. The patient’s antibodies were retested after 3 months and revealed persistently high titers confirming the diagnosis. APS management revolves around prevention of thrombotic events by anticoagulation.6In rare cases, catastrophic APS may cause multiple organ failure and be a fatal disease.7Though the infectious trigger remains unclear (EBV andBartonellaare possibilities), we suspect APS to be a driving factor in the patient’s presentation. The patient received therapeutically dosed enoxaparin and aspirin. Additionally, he received solumedrol intravenously with transition to oral prednisone. Retinal perfusion improved. Infectious disease was consulted and recommended a 4-week course of doxycycline and rifampin due to suspicion that the patient’s preceding febrile illness was secondary toBartonella. In follow-up, the patient’s right eye visual acuity remained stable at 20/25 with no new occlusions and gradual resolution of retinal lesions (Figure 2).

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 17-year-old male with an unremarkable medical history presented with 2 days of painless blurred vision in the right eye. Three weeks prior, he was admitted with fever, myalgias, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and truncal rash. Laboratory evaluation revealed leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Heterophile antibody test results were negative. He recovered with supportive treatment. On examination, the patient was well appearing. His best-corrected visual acuity in the affected right eye was 20/25 and baseline count fingers in the left, secondary to amblyopia. His intraocular pressures were normal and extraocular movements were full. Examination was notable for 1+ anterior chamber cell in the right eye. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated multifocal areas of retinal arteriolar and capillary nonperfusion, more so in the right eye than the left. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the right eye showed loss of inner retinal laminations, presumably due to intracellular swelling of the ganglion cell layer within areas of retinal arteriolar and capillary nonperfusion (Figure 1). Late vascular staining appeared limited to venules at the boundary of perfused and nonperfused retina and scattered areas of capillary nonperfusion. [Instruction]

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 13.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,

case_info.explanation: C. Order serologic infectious and inflammatory workup While most retinal artery occlusions are embolic, the current presentation is atypical. The patient experienced vision loss in his remaining good eye and inpatient workup may be prudent. Local steroid injection is not advisable before thorough systemic evaluation. Option D is lower yield considering the presentation. The patient was admitted for systemic evaluation. Branch retinal artery occlusions have a variety of etiologies, including embolic, vasospastic, vasculitic, and coagulopathic.1Older patients with embolic risk factors are the typical demographic. BRAOs are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population.2Carotid doppler, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging brain results were normal. Complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein results were normal. Blood cultures were negative. International normalized ratio was 1.2, mildly elevated. Partial thromboplastin time was normal. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) was considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions in a young patient without known risk factors. Testing revealed positive lupus anticoagulant and high titer β-2 glycoprotein immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) (>150 standard IgG and IgM units). Antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S activity were normal and factor V Leiden mutation was negative. Antinuclear antibody was positive at a low titer, 1:40. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. This patient presented 3 weeks after a febrile illness of uncertain etiology. A postinfectious process was suspected due to the timing of symptom onset and prompt resolution of systemic symptoms. An infectious workup was nonetheless initiated. Syphilis, tuberculosis, and toxoplasma serology results were negative.Bartonellawas considered due to the presence of retinal artery occlusions, history of lymphadenopathy, and substantial prior cat exposure.BartonellaIgG test results were positive (1:32 768 titer) and IgM results were negative. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgG results were positive (>750 U/mL viral capsid antigen antibody, 510 U/mL nuclear antibody) and IgM were negative. Cytomegalovirus IgG and HIV results were negative. West Nile Virus IgG and IgM were negative. APS is characterized by autoantibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and β-glycoprotein) with systemic thrombotic sequelae.3It can develop following systemic infections including HIV, cytomegalovirus, EBV, hepatitis, andBartonella.4The incidence of APS is approximately 5 in 100 000 persons per year.5The pathophysiology for development of APS is unclear. Furthermore, antibodies can be transient or persistent. The patient’s antibodies were retested after 3 months and revealed persistently high titers confirming the diagnosis. APS management revolves around prevention of thrombotic events by anticoagulation.6In rare cases, catastrophic APS may cause multiple organ failure and be a fatal disease.7Though the infectious trigger remains unclear (EBV andBartonellaare possibilities), we suspect APS to be a driving factor in the patient’s presentation. The patient received therapeutically dosed enoxaparin and aspirin. Additionally, he received solumedrol intravenously with transition to oral prednisone. Retinal perfusion improved. Infectious disease was consulted and recommended a 4-week course of doxycycline and rifampin due to suspicion that the patient’s preceding febrile illness was secondary toBartonella. In follow-up, the patient’s right eye visual acuity remained stable at 20/25 with no new occlusions and gradual resolution of retinal lesions (Figure 2).

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 17-year-old male with an unremarkable medical history presented with 2 days of painless blurred vision in the right eye. Three weeks prior, he was admitted with fever, myalgias, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and truncal rash. Laboratory evaluation revealed leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Heterophile antibody test results were negative. He recovered with supportive treatment. On examination, the patient was well appearing. His best-corrected visual acuity in the affected right eye was 20/25 and baseline count fingers in the left, secondary to amblyopia. His intraocular pressures were normal and extraocular movements were full. Examination was notable for 1+ anterior chamber cell in the right eye. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye revealed vitreous cell and a supratemporal branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) abutting the fovea. Multiple retinal nerve fiber layer infarcts were observed bilaterally throughout the posterior pole and retinal periphery. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated multifocal areas of retinal arteriolar and capillary nonperfusion, more so in the right eye than the left. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the right eye showed loss of inner retinal laminations, presumably due to intracellular swelling of the ganglion cell layer within areas of retinal arteriolar and capillary nonperfusion (Figure 1). Late vascular staining appeared limited to venules at the boundary of perfused and nonperfused retina and scattered areas of capillary nonperfusion. The patient denied intravenous drug use or antecedent trauma.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.
